newsitem.title: USA: Oxford, responding to consumers, reorganizes services.
newsitem.headline: Oxford, responding to consumers, reorganizes services.

text.p: Oxford Health Plans said Tuesday it was restructuring many of its services, including the creation an alternative medicine network and changing the way seriously ill patients are treated.

The health maintenance organisation, which is based in Norwalk, Conn., said that among other innovations, it was creating teams of specialists to treat serious conditions and would offer other, non-traditional forms of treatments that are usually not provided by HMOs.
"Consumer sentiment is decidedly in favour of greater choice and less restriction," Oxford Chairman Stephen Wiggins said in a statement announcing the new policy.
"Oxford is restructuring its systems to give our physicians and members more freedom to choose from a wider range of treatment options that will get them better and keep them healthy."
The company also expects to reduce medical costs through its new system because teams of speciality care providers will bid for the business.
"The speciality case management can lower cost by up to 20 percent per case, on average," Stephen Wiggins, chief executive officer of Oxford, said in an interview.
Analsyts also said Oxford's bottom line also will benefit.

"The savings could be substantial," said Christine Bennis, an analyst with UBS securities. "The teams should be able to bring down the cost of care, because the bids essentially fix the cost of an episode."

Oxford, which instituted the changes after polling its 1.7 million members, said that for certain medical categories "ranging from obstetrics to oncology" it would begin offering care by teams of physicians, therapists and other professionals who will be responsible for a patient's treatment from diagnosis through the conclusion of care.
The company said that more than 200 of the speciality care teams already had been formed and an additional 500 teams would be created this year.
In another consumer-oriented innovation Oxford said it would create a "performance profile" for each team to allow members to compare success rates for the procedures they are preparing to undergo.

Oxford also said it had created the country's first credentialed alternative medicine network, with roughly 1,500 acupuncturists, chiropractors, massage therapists, yoga instructors and nutritionists.

"Just as Oxford members have signalled their desire for greater freedom in seeking specialist services," the company said, "an internal survey made another demand clear: Almost one-third of Oxford members would like to seek treatment from an alternative practitioner, either as an adjunct to or as a replacement for conventional therapy."
The company also said that it had established a 24-hour, seven-days-a-week toll free hotline staffed by trained nurses that members can call to discuss symptoms and treatments.

It also is offering a Web site on the Internet that members will be able to use to check their benefits and the status of their claims, switch doctors and even look up the latest treatments in an extensive medical encyclopaedia.

Oxford also said that, in an effort to minimise administrative hassle, it would assign to each member a personal service agent who would be familiar with the customer's doctor, local hospital and benefits package.
"This is one person who knows your name, your history, your neighbourhood," the company said in its statement.
Oxford Health's stock closed at $63.325, up $1.875 on Nasdaq.
